preamble: The voiceless velar fricative [x] is replaced by the aspirated velar stop [kʰ], a fortition that keeps the voiceless velar place and turns continuous friction into a stop with an aspirated release. It arises chiefly where a language loses /x/ and merges it with an existing /kʰ/: in Thai the Sukhothai-era letter ฃ, which spelled a distinct velar fricative, fell together with ข [kʰ]; in Hindi, Persian and Arabic loans with /x/ are commonly nativized with /kʰ/ by speakers who lack the fricative.

examples.from: Sukhothai ฃาย (ฃ = velar fricative) 'to sell'
examples.note: The Ram Khamhaeng inscription (1283/1292) writes eleven words with ฃ, among them ฃาย 'sell', ฃวา 'right (side)', ฃุน 'lord' and เฃา 'mountain'; all are now spelled with ข and pronounced with [kʰ], and ฃ has no words in the 1999 Royal Institute Dictionary. Li (1977) reconstructs this series as Proto-Tai *x; Pittayaporn (2009) reconstructs the source as uvular *q, so the exact value of ฃ before the merger is debated.

Loanword nativization: outside careful educated speech, Hindi speakers commonly replace the borrowed fricative /x/ with native /kʰ/, and the nuqta-less spelling खबर reflects this; Wiktionary lists both /xə.bəɾ/ and /kʰə.bəɾ/.

sources: Pittayaporn, P. (2009). The Phonology of Proto-Tai. PhD dissertation, Cornell University. https://hdl.handle.net/1813/13855
Masica, C. P. (1991). The Indo-Aryan Languages. Cambridge University Press. https://www.cambridge.org/9780521299442
